preamble: Stopping of the emphatic interdental: Proto-Semitic *ṯ̣, reconstructed as an ejective dental fricative [θʼ], merged with the emphatic stop ṭ in Aramaic and, independently, in Soqotri. Old Aramaic still writes it with ṣ (𐤑𐤁𐤉 'gazelle'), Official Aramaic and later Aramaic with ṭ (𐡈𐡁𐡉, Syriac ṭabyā) (Militarev 2006); Wikipedia's correspondence table gives the Aramaic reflex as *ṱ, written ṣ, later ṭ. Soqotri lost all three interdentals, merging *θ, *ð and *θʼ with t, d and the emphatic t (Soqotri tˤarb 'piece of wood' where Mehri and Jibbali have θʼarb). Sources describe the result differently: Wikipedia's Proto-Semitic table gives the Soqotri merger partner as [tʼ], and its Soqotri article as [tˤ], adding that Soqotri emphatics were once ejective but, except /kʼ/, have largely become pharyngealized; Aramaic ṭēt is pharyngealized in the traditional pronunciations. The merger partner *ṭ is itself reconstructed as [tʼ], so the outcome here is the attested [tˤ], and the step [tʼ] > [tˤ] is filed separately. Plain *ṯ and *ḏ became t and d in the same two branches. The Proto-Semitic value is a reconstruction: whether the emphatics were ejective or pharyngealized is debated, since the daughter languages differ (pharyngealized in Arabic, Aramaic and Tiberian Hebrew, glottalized in Ethiopian Semitic and Modern South Arabian), though they are generally reconstructed as glottalized, i.e. ejective (Cantineau 1952; Kogan 2011: 61, as cited by Wikipedia; Wikipedia, Proto-Semitic language), but some reconstructions give *ṯ̣ a pharyngealized value [θˤ] or [ðˤ] (Wikipedia, Ẓāʾ), and 'maximal' affricate accounts make it [tθʼ]. This entry follows the [θʼ] of Wikipedia's Proto-Semitic consonant table.
